newsitem.title: USA: Calif. Governor vetoes bankruptcy oversight bill.
newsitem.headline: Calif. Governor vetoes bankruptcy oversight bill.

text.p: California Gov. Pete Wilson vetoed legislation that would have increased state oversight over local governments seeking bankruptcy protection, arguing that it is the responsibility of local officials to manage their own fiscal affairs.
Wilson, a Republican, vetoed Senate Bill 349, which would have established the Local Agency Bankruptcy Committee.
Under the measure, local agencies in the state that intended to file for bankruptcy would have had to seek the committee's approval before petitioning the courts.

"This bill would inappropriately vest responsibility for local fiscal affairs at the state level, creating an instrument of state government to usurp the authority of local officials to decide the wisdom of a bankruptcy filing, when the state has no responsibility or special capability to take whatever next steps might be required as an alternative," Wilson said in a statement.

"Further, vesting power on a Local Agency Bankruptcy Committee, made up of state officials, to approve or deny a municipality's bankruptcy request, could raise questions of the liability of the state to creditors of the public agency if eligibility for bankruptcy is denied," Wilson said.
State Treasurer Matt Fong had strongly urged Wilson to sign the legislation.
"Before a local agency takes such a serious step as bankruptcy, that so dramatically affects the state, state level oversight should occur," Fong said.
Fong argued that the legislation could help to lower issuance costs in the state.

"Every time that I go back to Wall Street, they're still scared to death that somebody out here is going to pull the trigger and go file for bankruptcy," Fong said last month. "There is a payment that's being made because, in California, we still have the right to pull the trigger unilaterally."
The measure was introduced in the wake of Orange County, Calif.,'s unprecedented bankruptcy filing.

Orange County filed for protection under Chapter 9 of the federal Bankruptcy Code on Dec. 6, 1994, after sustaining investment losses of more than $1.6 billion. The county emerged from bankruptcy in June of this year.
The state's Department of Finance was opposed to the legislation.
